item.title: Animated Ultraviolet Holography via Programmable Nonlinear Phase Transfer
item.description: arXiv:2611.00267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dynamic and programmable control of ultraviolet (UV) light remains challenging because of conventional high material absorption and the limited functionality of optics such as lenses, mirrors or filters, and optoelectronic devices, such as spatial phase modulators, over the UV range. Here, by employing the concept of virtual metasurfaces based on arrays of programmable optical patterns on a 600-nm-thick lithium niobate film as the nonlinear medium, we demonstrate nonlinear phase transfer, generating programmable holography in the UV range. This arrangement provides a unique platform for generating animated holograms. A spatial light modulator encodes a computer-generated phase distribution onto a longer-wavelength pump beam, while second-harmonic generation transfers the programmed spatial phase to the UV field through the quadratic nonlinear interaction. Importantly, the nonlinear film serves as a simple frequency-conversion interface, eliminating the need for nanostructure patterning or direct UV spatial modulation. By incorporating the nonlinear phase relationship into the hologram design, we experimentally reconstruct six distinct UV holographic patterns, with normalised cross-correlation values ranging from 0.68 to 0.83, demonstrating reliable UV holographic image reconstruction. As a result, the dynamic updating of the SLM enables animated UV holograms at 10 Hz, demonstrating reconfigurable UV holography using the same nonlinear film. The system also supports tunable SHG emission from 350 to 390 nm and dynamic beam steering at approximately 20 Hz. The results demonstrate the potential of virtual metasurfaces to realise software-defined UV holography by transferring spatial programming across optical frequencies. This opens new opportunities for reconfigurable short-wavelength UV beam shaping and structured illumination, without the need for UV-compatible optics or optoelectronics.

item.title: Coherent transduction and dynamical back-action between light and millimeter waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.00279v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Electro-optic transduction can bypass the loss and noise of electronic frequency conversion at millimeter-wave frequencies by parametrically converting signals onto low-loss, low-noise optical carriers, with coupling rates that grow with frequency. Exploiting this growth, however, requires shrinking both the millimeter-wave and optical resonators while preserving their quality factors and spatial overlap, which has not yet been achieved. Here, we demonstrate a triply resonant transducer whose optical and millimeter-wave resonators have comparable dimensions and minimal mode volumes. Coupled lithium niobate Fabry-P\'erot cavities, with free spectral ranges above 650 GHz and quality factors up to $10^6$, form a photonic molecule integrated with a quarter-wave gold resonator at 263 GHz. The device reaches a vacuum electro-optic coupling rate $g_0/2\pi \approx 60$ kHz, six times larger than previous millimeter-wave transducers and sixty times larger than at microwave frequencies. The device optically detects room-temperature thermal millimeter-wave photons at effective occupancies below one, which also serve as a calibration tone for transduction efficiency. Coherent transduction reaches cooperativities approaching 0.3, corresponding to internal efficiencies around 67%, accompanied by electro-optic dynamical back-action that broadens or narrows the optical resonances. These results demonstrate the advantage and feasibility of the frequency scaling of electro-optic coupling, establishing an architecture for weak-signal sensing and quantum and classical networking.

item.title: BEEF: A Hybrid Integrated Photonic Simulation Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.00393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A Python framework is presented that retains first-principles electromagnetic modeling while extending simulation to devices whose length and geometric complexity place them beyond the practical reach of either method alone. The Bridged Engine for eigenmode expansion (EME) and finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) (BEEF) partitions a device into sections which are simulated using either EME or FDTD independently developed Maxwell solvers depending on what best suits each section's geometry, and cascades the resulting responses. BEEF calibrates the EME propagation constants against FDTD-measured phase accumulation, providing a mode identity verification diagnostic across solver interfaces. For a 2x2 multimode-interference splitter, the hybrid result agrees with full-device FDTD to within 0.59% (bar) and 0.76% (cross) across the C-band; a tapered variant agrees to within 0.87% and 2.01%, respectively. For a directional coupler, effective-index calibration reduces cut-position dependence 167-fold. A circuit-level cascade reproduces the measured Fabry-Perot resonance lineshape and free spectral range while exploring the coupler-length and arm-length design plane through post-processing of four cached simulations. Finally, we use BEEF to simulate a 167.3 um-long 4x4 MMI-based 90-degree optical hybrid that is computationally impractical for full-device FDTD, with a reduced-length variant confirming close agreement in transmission and relative phase.

item.title: Nonperturbative theory of thin-vapor-layer linear optical properties: towards the optimal design of alkali-metal vapor nanocells
item.description: arXiv:2611.00400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hot alkali-metal vapors confined inside nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells are highly suitable media for miniature and cheap frequency standards, magnetometers and atomic sensors. Yet, their linear optical properties in case of low to moderate atomic densities are not fully understood. The primary reason for that is the complex, strongly nonlocal optical response of such systems to the incident resonant radiation arising as the result of the free motion of atoms and their collisions with the walls. To date, calculations of reflection and transmission spectra of these cells has been restricted to perturbation theory in atomic density for the case of quenching atom-wall collisions, which substantially limited the scope of their practical applications. Here we introduce the rigorous numerical approach for computing thin-vapor-layer spectra with an accurate account for the nonlocal optical response at arbitrary optical density and layer thickness. Our model predicts a density-dependent blue shift of the resonance that is absent in the first-order perturbative description. We show that its values are comparable to the natural linewidth of an atomic transition and, therefore, too large to be neglected in most use cases. Inspired by recent experiments, we then explore a wide range of vapor layer thicknesses and study how the reflectivity and its derivative with respect to the laser detuning depend on the layer thickness. Finally, we derive an approximate expression for the thickness at which the first derivative of the reflectivity reaches its maximum that agrees closely with the rigorous numerical model and reduces to the first-order analytical result. These results provide a practical design tool for nanometer-thick spectroscopic cells in different applications as well as a starting point for further development of the theory.

item.title: Experimental demonstration of response-enhanced fiber Sagnac gyroscopy via imaginary weak-value amplification
item.description: arXiv:2611.00481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We experimentally demonstrate a 100-m long fiber Sagnac gyroscope employing imaginary weak-value amplification (IWVA) to enhance the optical readout response to rotation. A Sagnac-induced polarization phase is converted into a measurable spectral response through polarization post-selection and spectrally resolved detection. By varying the post-selection angle, we characterize the gyroscope response over the experimentally accessible rotation-rate range. The response increases systematically toward orthogonal post-selection, yielding a maximum experimental enhancement of approximately 13 times relative to a fixed reference configuration without postselection. Fast Fourier transform and Allan-deviation measurements further characterize the noise and stability of the gyroscope. Near-orthogonal post-selection reduces the equivalent rotation-rate fluctuations, with the minimum Allan deviation decreasing from $0.06~\mathrm{rad/s}$ for the reference configuration to $0.0091~\mathrm{rad/s}$ for the configuration exhibiting the maximum response enhancement, corresponding to an approximately 6.6-fold reduction. Low-frequency fluctuations of the broadband superluminescent diode source limit the long-term stability. These results demonstrate that IWVA provides a practical approach for response-enhanced fiber-based Sagnac gyroscopy and precision rotation sensing.

item.title: Non-Hermitian Theory of Surface Emitting Jackiw-Rebbi States
item.description: arXiv:2611.00674v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Topological interface states in open photonic systems combine spatial localization at domain walls with temporal confinement characterized by a radiative quality factor. Here, we develop a non-Hermitian Dirac formalism for surface-emitting Jackiw-Rebbi states in dielectric metagratings. We show how varying the local amplitude of the lattice perturbation shapes the complex Dirac mass profile, enabling control over the quality factors and far-field radiation patterns of the interface states, while preserving their topological character. Applying this framework to a metagrating with second-order Brillouin-zone folding, we design a spatially graded superlattice perturbation that supports interface states with quality factors exceeding 10$^4$ and Hermite-Gaussian beam emission. These results establish superlattice perturbations as a strategy for topological beam shaping and offer a route toward high-Q topological surface emitters.

item.title: Energy-Centroid Trembling near Exceptional Points in Photonic Time Crystals
item.description: arXiv:2611.00743v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In a photonic time crystal with a modulated Lorentz restoring coefficient, modulation reweights the potential energy of the polarization and loss drains its kinetic energy; when these sectors are offset within a pulse, the energy centroid trembles in every cycle while the Poynting-flux velocity stays bounded. Near the gap-edge exceptional point the mode geometry amplifies these offsets, and for a narrow-band pulse on one passband Floquet branch the trembling-velocity amplitude generically grows as the inverse square root of the momentum detuning, rounded by finite bandwidth. Loss modulated in phase or in antiphase with the restoring coefficient can change the trembling coefficient while the band-slope and Petermann coefficients barely move. In the lossy example studied, a forward field pulse launched with the polarization at rest exhibits delayed bursts near the beat recurrence after substantial energy loss, with monochromatic amplitudes following the inverse three-halves power of the detuning over the computed range. Intracycle energy exchange and preparation thus shape the centroid motion beyond what the band slope and the Floquet Petermann factor determine.
item.dc:creator: Kyungmin Lee, Younsung Kim, Minwook Kyung, Seungmin Yeon, Bumki Min

item.title: Semi-classical analysis of noise squeezing in Kerr microresonators
item.description: arXiv:2611.00805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Kerr microresonators are integrated nonlinear devices widely used to generate classical optical frequency combs and nonclassical states of light. In particular, they provide a promising platform for squeezed light sources, which are important elements of emerging quantum sensing, communication, and computing technologies. Designing such sources requires numerical tools that efficiently incorporate realistic device physics and noise processes. Here, we show that established semi-classical frameworks based on the Lugiato-Lefever equation and the Ikeda map, instrumental in the development of classical light sources, can also predict the quadrature-noise properties of squeezed light when vacuum fluctuations are properly included. We consider three canonical configurations producing two-mode quadrature squeezing, single-mode quadrature squeezing, and intensity difference squeezing. In each case, the semi-classical simulations produce quadrature variances and noise spectra in close agreement with the quantum theoretical predictions. These frameworks therefore provide practical tools for designing squeezed light sources, with the capability to incorporate additional noise mechanisms, nonlinear effects, and complex resonator arrangements. More fundamentally, our results show that key experimental signatures of squeezing can be modeled as phase-sensitive amplification of properly normalized vacuum fluctuations within stochastic semi-classical field equations. This observation helps distinguish squeezing properties accessible through semi-classical field evolution from those intrinsically requiring a full quantum description.

item.title: Unlocking Low-Frequency Laser Doppler Holography Spectra for Functional Retinal and Choroidal Microvascular Phenotyping
item.description: arXiv:2611.01052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The low-frequency part of optical fluctuation spectra recorded by laser Doppler holography at a frame rate of 37~kHz is typically filtered out to reveal functional blood-flow waveforms in major retinal and choroidal vessels. We construct a time-varying spectral-excess (SE) distribution in capillary-associated territories by selecting complete cardiac cycles and applying successive spatial and beat medians in regions where vessels are unresolved and intermittent eye motion can dominate the signal. At each phase, spectral excess compares the integrated Doppler spectral area between two fixed low-frequency peaks near $\pm2$~kHz with a reference area defined by the high-frequency tail near $\pm18.5$~kHz. The resulting waveform, displayed against normalized cardiac phase, retains variation throughout the cardiac cycle and provides a basis for exploring its temporal organization. We summarize spectral-excess strength by the spectral excess index (SEI), defined as the temporal median of SE, and also describe an alternative evaluation after spectral pooling. A representative recording illustrates the construction. Physiological specificity and repeatability remain to be quantified.
