item.title: Reciprocity Violation for Mie Scatterers at the Interface and a Scattering Solar Concentrator
item.description: arXiv:2307.06711v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: It is shown that reciprocity of the optical path can be violated through asymmetric strength coupling via near-field from resonant Mie scatterers to total internal reflection modes in a dielectric slab. Numerical simulations for silicon nanospheres separated by a nanogap from the glass substrate reveal that at least two orders of magnitude rectification ratio can be realized for such an optical diode configuration. Implementation to a solar light harvesting device, a scattering solar concentrator, is discussed, indicating a similar efficiency is achievable as for the state-of-the-art devices based on luminescence.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Sychugov

item.title: An integrated photonic millimeter-wave receiver with sub-ambient noise temperature
item.description: arXiv:2510.06176v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Growing demands for timing precision in positioning systems, and resolution in atmospheric sensing and automotive radar, have extended receiver frontends into the millimetre-wave and THz regimes. At these frequencies, the noise performance of field-effect transistors used in low-noise amplifiers degrades rapidly due to parasitic effects, limited carrier mobility, hot electrons, and shot noise. Parametric transducers that couple electromagnetic signals to optical fields can offer quantum-limited sensitivity at room temperature. Electro-optic materials can enable receivers that transduce radiofrequency signals into optical phase shifts. Yet to date, room-temperature receivers using electro-optical detection have not attained a noise figure comparable to the electronic amplifiers. Here we demonstrate a room-temperature cavity electro-optic-based millimetre-wave receiver on a lithium tantalate photonic integrated circuit, achieving an on-chip photon-number transduction efficiency of 10%. The equivalent input-referred receiver-added noise temperatures reach $110\,\mathrm{K}$ on-chip and $202^{+35}_{-33}\,\mathrm{K}$ for the full system at 60.5 GHz, with noise figure matching state-of-the-art V-band electronic low-noise amplifiers. We resolve the thermal noise in cavity electro-optic transducers, showing that the system is limited by thermal photon occupation ($\sim$100) in the millimetre-wave cavity and optical vacuum noise, with no measurable excess noise. Our work demonstrates that integrated photonics can reach state-of-the-art electronic receiver noise performance while offering high-radiofrequency-power survivability and compatibility with remote optical readout. This establishes cavity electro-optics as a low-noise, electromagnetic interference-resilient, chip-scale receiver frontend for millimetre-wave applications, enabling scalable analogue processing in the optical domain.
item.dc:creator: Junyin Zhang, Shuhang Zheng, Jiachen Cai, Connor Denney, Zihan Li, Yichi Zhang, Changhao Han, Xin Ou, Gabriel Santamaria-Botello, Tobias J. Kippenberg

item.title: On Sub-Sevenfold Symmetries in LH2 Stacked Ring Scaffolds: A Quantum Optical Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2603.23743v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For highly efficient light-harvesting, purple photosynthetic bacteria rely on light-harvesting 2 (LH2) complexes featuring ninefold, eightfold, and sevenfold rotational symmetries; however, sub-sevenfold scaffolds have not yet been observed in nature. To investigate this absence, we utilize a closed coupled-dipole model that neglects dissipative effects, which remains valid for a temporal window shorter than the interlayer excitation energy transfer time (on the picosecond scale) in an LH2 scaffold. We examine collective eigenmodes across $C_n$ stacked model ring geometries for $n=9,8,7,6$. Our results demonstrate that the minimum energy separation between specific collective bands occurs at the angular-momentum modes $m=\pm 1$ for known geometries, effectively predicting the photoactive absorption wavelengths of the lower bacteriochlorophyll (BChl) ring. Specifically, we predict peaks at 851, 848, and 825 nm for ninefold, eightfold, and sevenfold symmetries, respectively, which agree well with experimental observations. Applying this analysis to a hypothetical sixfold geometry, we predict a significant blue shift in the photoactive wavelength of the lower BChl ring, suggesting inefficient harvesting of the available solar spectrum and offering a quantum optical perspective on the evolutionary absence of sub-sevenfold scaffolds in LH2 complexes. Our study demonstrates that quantum cooperative models can elucidate specific aspects of biological LH systems.
item.dc:creator: Arpita Pal

item.title: Noise-resilient nanophotonic gyroscope with sub-prad phase resolution
item.description: arXiv:2604.00459v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Optical gyroscopes based on the Sagnac effect are the cornerstone of precision orientation and navigation. However, their bulky form factors prevent deployment in emerging mobile and autonomous systems. On nanophotonic platforms, the Sagnac signal plummets under aggressive miniaturization. Consequently, the signal is easily swamped by refractive-index fluctuations, rendering navigation-grade sensitivity within just a few square millimeters a notoriously elusive goal. Here, we demonstrate a noise-resilient nanophotonic optical gyroscope by exploiting a two-chain decoupling architecture to effectively isolate the rotation signal from channel noise. Implemented on a 3 mm^2 passive silicon-nitride chip, the proof-of-concept device achieves a bias instability of 0.79 deg/h and an angle random walk of 0.0014 deg/\sqrt{h}, representing improvements of 4 and 6 orders of magnitude, respectively, over a representative nanophotonic gyroscope with the same enclosed sensing area (ref. 1). In the broader context of integrated optical gyroscopes, our approach bridges the long-standing size-performance gap by two to three orders of magnitude, moving chip-scale devices into a previously inaccessible regime and pointing toward navigation-relevant precision for monolithic microsystems. This architecture further enables an estimated input-equivalent phase resolution of 0.17 prad with general applicability, establishing a foundational framework for the next generation of robust, monolithically integrated photonic sensing systems.
item.dc:creator: Yu Tao, Xinhang Li, Jingzheng Huang, Zidi Lin, Yuyao Guo, Hongjing Li, Linjie Zhou, Guihua Zeng

item.title: Gaussian pulse scattering by a chiral spherical shell
item.description: arXiv:2604.21466v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Theory was formulated for scattering by a coated chiral sphere of a plane wave of arbitrary polarization state with amplitude modulated by a Gaussian pulse. The spherical core and the concentric shell of the sphere were composed of two different homogeneous materials, both isotropic chiral. Calculations of energy efficiencies for extinction, total scattering, and absorption were carried out for the shell material with experimentally determined constitutive parameters, the core being vacuous. All three energy efficiencies depend on the relative thickness of the shell and the circular polarization state of the carrier plane wave.
item.dc:creator: Hector M. Iga-Buitron, Tom G. Mackay, Akhlesh Lakhtakia

item.title: Biting fly vision and zebra stripes
item.description: arXiv:2605.17049v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The function of the zebras striped coat has been discussed since Darwin and Wallace. Increasing amount of comparative and experimental evidence supports the hypothesis that the stripes mainly serve as protection against visually orienting biting Diptera, in particular tabanids (horse flies), glossinids (tsetse flies), and culicids (mosquitoes). The proposed ways this protection works include polarotactic disruption and silhouette break-up, as well as motion based illusions in motion based detectors of the insect visual system. In this work a complementary purely optical mechanism is presented to explain why the zebra's stripe pattern provides a measurable advantage in warding off biting flies. We have quantified the optical illusion caused by the interaction between the zebra's striped coat and the fly's compound eye with a linear, shift-invariant Fourier model based on published optical data of the diurnal Culicidae. The model predicts that, within an approach range of about 1-5 m, the interaction of the stripe pattern with the ommatidial sampling produces parasitic spatial frequencies that are absent from the physical stimulus. These frequencies fall within the range most important for host fixation and controlling their landing. A post-retinal motion-detector shows that these parasitic frequencies create misleading motion signals. The magnitude of this parasitic energy predicts the specific loss of the radial-expansion (looming) cue that gates landing, linking the optical disturbance quantitatively to the motion computation that controls the fly's final approach. By rigorously modeling visual processes and quantifying disturbances, this study makes a decisive contribution to clarifying the role of zebra stripes in defense against biting flies.
item.dc:creator: Krispin M. Dettlaff

item.title: Absolute Experimental Measurement of Intrinsic Helicity in Elementary Plasmonic Nanostructures
item.description: arXiv:2605.26058v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Helicity is a universal quantity describing the internal rotation of an object or a field. Whether it characterizes fundamental properties such as the spin of elementary particles or leads to practical consequences such as the toxicity or harmlessness of chiral molecules, defining and measuring it is essential. However, this remains ambiguous in the case of chiral photonic systems such as plasmonic nanoparticles or photonic metasurfaces, where contrary to common knowledge, the observation of circularly polarized dependent optical properties is not a relevant measure for the helicity. We demonstrate experimentally and theoretically that the helicity can be rigorously defined and measured in a nanoplasmonics system emitting circularly polarized light after excitation in the near-field by a focused electron beam. In the case of a model system composed of two plasmonic dipoles (Born-Kuhn systems), we show that the helicity of photonic modes takes on a very intuitive form and can be simply measured by symmetrizing the geometry of excitation and detection. The method could be extended to a variety of chiral photonic systems, whose locally enhanced properties make them promising for the engineering of local chirality.
item.dc:creator: Malo B\'ezard, Simon Garrigou, J\'er\'emie B\'eal, Andreas Horrer, Yves Auad, Hugo Louren\c{c}o-Martins, Davy G\'erard, Mathieu Kociak

item.title: Two Photon excitation microscopy of individual Single-Walled Carbon Nanotubes
item.description: arXiv:2607.05129v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Two-photon fluorescence imaging achieves deep-tissue penetration through long excitation wavelengths and nonlinear excitation confinement. The 1700 nm transparency window is particularly attractive, as it optimally balances tissue scattering and absorption. However, efficient fluorophores for two-photon excitation in this window remain limited. Moreover the weak near-infrared emission of individual emitters, and the low photon detection efficiency, has so far precluded single-particle imaging. Here, we characterize the two-photon excitation properties of chirality-sorted pristine and quantum color center-functionalized single-walled carbon nanotubes under 1700 nm excitation. By measuring and comparing their two-photon action cross-sections, we identify quantum color center-functionalized (6,5) nanotubes emitting at 1140 nm, as the most promising emitter, with an exceptionally large cross-section of (57 \pm 2).103 GM. Leveraging these favorable photophysical properties, we image individual nanotubes under 1700 nm excitation, to our knowledge the first demonstration of single-particle imaging at this wavelength. These results establish quantum color center-functionalized (6,5) nanotube as a strong candidate for long-wavelength two-photon imaging and lay the groundwork for deep-tissue single-particle imaging.
item.dc:creator: Nasim Akhtar, Marc Tondusson, Benjamin Flavel, St\'ephane Bancelin, Laurent Cognet

item.title: Learning qBIC Resonances across Metasurface Families in Dielectric Fourier Space
item.description: arXiv:2610.11500v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BIC) metasurfaces are typically described by geometry-specific parameters, hindering cross-geometry comparison, while ultranarrow quasi-BIC (qBIC) features are easily diluted in full-spectrum learning. Here, we map 2,015 samples from seven dielectric metasurface families onto a shared reciprocal-lattice grid. Two fixed low-order Fourier descriptors capture within-branch resonance shifts, with mean $R^2$ values of 0.871-0.999. Field-level analysis of two representative branches shows that these shifts are consistent with the Maxwell-Fourier perturbation picture. A five-channel Fourier-space backbone models the broadband spectrum. A local resonance expert uses complex Fourier coefficients to parameterize the qBIC resonance through a differentiable Fano layer. The expert reduces resonance-position mean absolute error (MAE) from 3.2 to 0.95 nm and reduces the minimum-transmission MAE by a factor of 14 on a geometry-blocked test set. The same coordinate supports spectrum-to-structure reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: Shuangteng Lei, Li Yu, Tianxin Li, Wei Lu

item.title: Reconfigurable Free-Space Optical Interconnects
item.description: arXiv:2610.30757v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Free-space optical interconnects can support many low-data-rate channels while avoiding the cost, energy consumption, and packaging constraints of optical waveguide- or fiber-based systems that are widely used today. We propose a free-space optical interconnect system based on reconfigurable micromirror arrays, and show that it scales favorably due to its two-dimensional scaling. We discuss the channel count scaling model, compare our demonstration with theory, and project a channel count above 10,000 to achieve 100 Tbps with slow channels (e.g., <10 Gbps). In a proof-of-concept system with a piston-motion micromirror array, we demonstrate nine channels that are simultaneously optimized. The optimization enables -21.7 dB of average worst-case crosstalk for a channel pitch equal to twice the beam radius, a smaller channel spacing than that required in flat tip-tilt mirrors. The optimization flow is further investigated for different channel spacings, simultaneous illumination, and different numbers of outputs, which generally achieve smaller worst-case crosstalk than the flat tip-tilt mirror case. Overall, the work demonstrates the advantage of piston-motion micromirrors in the proposed optical interconnects.
item.dc:creator: Jaekwon Lee, Carson G. Valdez, Anne R. Kroo, David A. B. Miller, Olav Solgaard

item.title: Deep-Microscopic Photonic Bandstructure of a Two-Dimensional Honeycomb Lattice
item.description: arXiv:2610.33709v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conventional descriptions of light in materials rely on macroscopic models that average the optical response over the microscopic lattice structures. These models are deployed in the semi-classical limit, where the collective local response over many lattice sites is adequate. However, they fail to capture the full spatial dispersion, which requires a lattice-resolved description of light. We address this limitation by formulating a deep-microscopic nonlocal theory of the photon based on the Maxwell Hamiltonian and its characteristic equation. The solution reveals the full spatial dispersion in the form of deep-microscopic photonic bandstructure, and corresponding real-space Bloch field textures. We demonstrate our theory for a two-dimensional (2D) tight-binding model of a gapped honeycomb lattice. Our framework thus extends photons to the same microscopic footing as electrons or phonons, providing a unified route to studying topology, dissipation, and quantum fluctuations of light in dispersive materials.
item.dc:creator: Pronoy Das, Sathwik Bharadwaj, Wenbo Sun, Zubin Jacob

item.title: Periodic orbits underlying optical turbulence in the Lugiato-Lefever equation
item.description: arXiv:2509.10283v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optical turbulence in driven nonlinear resonators is a form of spatiotemporal chaos that remains poorly understood and is largely characterized through simulations and experiments but lacks a dynamical-systems description. Here we show that in the regime of weak spatiotemporal chaos, the dynamics is structured by families of exact, fully nonlinear, time-periodic solutions of the Lugiato-Lefever equation for driven-dissipative Kerr resonators. These unstable periodic orbits, which we term Oscillating Turing Rolls (OTR), are embedded within the spatiotemporal chaos of optical turbulence. Parametric continuation using Newton-Krylov methods reveals their existence range, stability, and bifurcation-theoretic origin. In symmetry-constrained domains, OTR solutions are intermittently shadowed by chaotic trajectories; in extended domains, they appear as localized motifs of spatiotemporal chaos. Identifying these nonlinear, non-chaotic building blocks establishes a dynamical-systems-based description of optical turbulence in nonlinear optical resonators.
item.dc:creator: Andrey Gelash, Savyaraj Deshmukh, Andrey Shusharin, Tobias M. Schneider, Tobias J. Kippenberg

item.title: Breakdown of Fluctuational Electrodynamics in the Extreme Near Field
item.description: arXiv:2606.05845v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Fluctuational electrodynamics relies on the assumption that thermal fluctuations in distinct bodies are statistically independent. It is shown that this approximation breaks down in the extreme near-field regime, where hybridization of surface phonon-polaritons across nanometric vacuum gaps generates finite fluctuating-current cross correlations between opposite interfaces. Using a microscopic coupled-oscillator model combined with a Green-tensor formulation of the Poynting vector, the resulting correlation-induced correction to radiative heat transfer is derived. For polar materials, these correlations become significant when the hybridization energy approaches the intrinsic damping rate and can substantially modify conventional fluctuational-electrodynamics predictions at subnanometric separations.
item.dc:creator: Philippe Ben-Abdallah

item.title: Quantifying Ultrafast Orbital Pumping and Nanometre-Scale Orbital Diffusion in Magnetic Heterostructures
item.description: arXiv:2608.29165v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Quantifying ultrafast orbital pumping and transport remains challenging because spin and orbital currents contribute coherently to terahertz emission. Here, we combine spintronic terahertz emission spectroscopy with wedge-sample thickness control to disentangle these contributions in Fe, Co and Ni heterostructures with Ta, W and Nb. Their opposite spin Hall and orbital Hall polarities enable quantitative determination of relative pumping strengths and propagation lengths. We find that orbital pumping increases from Fe to Ni, with inferred orbital-to-spin current ratios reaching several tens of percent in Ni, exceeding current microscopic predictions. Remarkably, Nb exhibits an orbital diffusion length of ~1.5 nm, substantially longer than in Ta and W and beyond the sub-nanometre scale predicted by recent orbital-relaxation calculations. These findings provide quantitative experimental benchmarks for ultrafast orbital pumping and transport.
item.dc:creator: Tongyang Guan, Jiahao Liu, Yuxiao Mo, Liangliang Zhu, Yizheng Wu, Zhensheng Tao

item.title: Making Weak Interlayer Excitons Absorb via Purcell Engineering of Critical Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2610.20307v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Interlayer excitons (IXs) in transition metal dichalcogenide bilayers possess unique dipolar properties, providing a path for exploring correlated many-body phases, electrically tunable dipole-dipole interactions, and long-range exciton transport. However, the large electron-hole separation underlying their dipolar character also results in a significantly reduced oscillator strength, limiting their direct optical interaction with light, and thus the direct probing of their dynamics and many-body interactions. Here, we show that by using Purcell engineering of critical coupling, a weak interlayer transition can absorb as strongly as the dominant intralayer transition, despite its much smaller intrinsic oscillator strength. Using this approach, in an open cavity architecture we demonstrate an order of magnitude IX absorption modulation in bilayer and trilayer MoS2, with doubling of the IX to A-exciton interaction strength weight from ~23% to ~53%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that in a tailored closed cavity architecture, the IX enhancement can reach beyond an order of magnitude, from ~5% to ~83% excitonic absorption, enabling IX absorption similar to intralayer excitons. An analytical description of the interaction is obtained via a closed-form transmission-line model which separates the excitonic and photonic contributions to the optical response, revealing how cavity architecture can be designed towards critical coupling. Our findings establish Purcell engineering of critical coupling as a general route to controlling and enhancing weak excitonic transitions.
item.dc:creator: Saroj Poudyal, Anabel Atash Kahlon, Michael Klein, Matan Meshulam, Yonatan Gershuni, Thomas Poirier, James H. Edgar, Mukesh Kumar, Seth Ariel Tongay, Itai Epstein

item.title: Nonclassicality from Incomplete Fock-State Statistics
item.description: arXiv:2610.32908v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Nonclassicality in bosonic systems can be certified directly from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction. To complete a library of such criteria we introduce a numerical framework that constructs optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses from arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities by solving a semi-infinite linear program. The method contains known analytical criteria as special cases while generally detecting substantially larger nonclassical regions. We provide an open-source implementation of the numerical optimization together with the analytical criteria discussed here, enabling direct application of the framework to measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms. As a case study, we apply it to the resonant Jaynes--Cummings model with thermal states and reveal nonclassicality at short interaction times and close to thermal balance, where detection of nonclassicality is otherwise challenging.
item.dc:creator: Martin \v{Z}onda, Pavel Bal\'a\v{z}, Luk\'a\v{s} Lachman, Darren W. Moore, Tom\'a\v{s} Novotn\'y, Radim Filip

item.title: Characteristics of VHF and UHF band detection using Stark shifting in Rydberg-atom sensors
item.description: arXiv:2610.40952v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a characterization of the sensitivity of broadband electric field measurements in the Very High Frequency (VHF) and Ultra High Frequency (UHF) bands using AC stark shifting of Rydberg states. The dependence of the sensitivity and dynamic range of the field measurements using nD5/2 states of cesium for principal quantum numbers n= 60, 70, 80, 90 and 100 is presented, detailing the intricacies involved. The frequencies considered for the measurement range from 50 MHz to 900 MHz for which a transverse electromagnetic (TEM) cell is used to excite the Rydberg atoms with the RF fields. The relative sensitivities achieved for various principal quantum numbers are presented. A general trend of better sensitivity for higher principal quantum numbers is observed. This work paves the way for a better understanding of the AC Stark dependent field measurements using Rydberg sensors.
